description.narrative: Insatsen syftar till att bidra till övergångsprocessen genom att genomföra demokratistärkande åtgärder som främjar reformen av det colombianska valsystemet genom att; 1) Stärka samhällsorganisationer och lokala institutioner under övergångsprocessen genom åtgärder som syftar till att stärka informationsprocesser och initiativtagande hos medborgare; 2) Stärka lokala institutioner genom bättre förståelse av korruption associerat till det colombianska valsystemet; 3) Påverka reformprocesser som syftar till att stärka demokratin. Programmet får 11197 645 SEK mellan åren 2017-2021.

The intervention aims to contribute to the transition process towards the democratic strengthening through actions that promote the modernization of the Colombian electoral system by 1) Strengthening social organizations and local institutions during the transition process, through actions aimed to reinforce information processes, formation, and citizen action. 2) Strengthening local institutions through a better comprehension of corruption phenomena associated to the political-electoral system. 3) Influence reform processes of political and electoral matter, aiming for the strengthening of democracy. The program will receive 11 197 645 SEK between 2017-2021.

This project aimed at contributing to the process of transition towards democratic strengthening by promoting the modernization of the Colombian electoral system and the expansion of local and daily democracy. This includes three main outputs:
1.Transition and democratic strengthening: it includes the electoral observation process, that will produce informational risk maps; the characterization of social dynamics of the post-conflict zones; and democratic quality assessment, that includes womens role in national and local politics, and the everyday democratic citizen participation.
2.Corruption, politics, and democracy: This objective seeks to strengthen the local institutions by offering a bigger comprehension of the corruption phenomena, associated to the political-electoral system and to create accountability measures between the elected officers and their voters.
3.Political influence society-state: The last objective aims to influence in the legal reforms and institutional adjustments that are required for the post-conflict scenario in political and electoral thematic. Those actions will be supported in the research and analysis that the MOE performs throughout the country.

As regards the first output, during the activity period (2017-10-01 - 2021-12-31) 3 national elections were held: March 2018 for the election of Congress (august 2018-2022) and May 2018 for the election of the Colombian President. October 27, 2019, for the election of local authorities for the period January 2020 to December 2023. In addition, there were 19 atypical elections to replace mayors (6 in 2017, 7 in 2020, 6 in 2021), 4 popular consultations, 7 revocations of the mandate and the first ever election of Youth Municipal Councils (YMC) in Colombia, held on December the 5th 2021. MOE developed 335 electoral trainings with more than 6300 volunteers and 35 regional organizations and a total of 14,600 observers were deployed for the days of elections.
Watch Your Vote (Pilas con el Voto) is a tool that promotes citizen oversight through a massive media campaign and a system for receiving complaints that is handled jointly by the communications area and the legal office. During the activity period, 10.324 complaints were received for irregularities through www.pilasconelvoto.com MOE documented the most relevant cases that were sent to the General Attorneys Office and the Prosecutors General Office. The first institution opened 1824 investigations and captured 68 people for electoral irregularities.
The MOE has systematized electoral data and has carried out pre-electoral and post-election analyzes to give an overview of local governance. These data have been updated and published in a physical and virtual way with free and free access in the Electoral Political Information System - www.datoselectorales.org which is a mechanism that allows the publication of relevant information on electoral matters.
The Observatory of Political and Social Violence of the MOE has monitored the threats, kidnappings, disappearances, attacks and murders committed against: candidates for elected office, elected officials, senior officials of the administrations at the national, departmental and municipal levels, political leaders and party leaders; and since 2016, also against social leaders and members of Community Action Boards (JAC), of each municipality of the country. In the activity period, MOE presented 27 reports of political violence.
Electoral Risk Maps were prepared for the 2018 Congress and Presidency elections, as well as for the 2019 local elections. In 2018 MOE analyzed 7 risk factors that covered from electoral institutions, electoral crime, factors of violence (especially political violence against social leaders), financing of the policy, peace agreement, special attention groups (such as indigenous and afro-descendant), communication (surveys and false news, among others). An emphasis was placed on post-conflict territories by focusing on four variables that may affect elections in these municipalities: electoral census vs. Population census, lack of access to polling stations as a risk to democratic participation, absenteeism and spatial electoral accessibility, and illicit crops and illegal mining: the illegal economy as a risk for electoral transparency. In 2019 MOE analyzed political violence in 8 regions and received widespread media coverage. These maps were featured 456 times in 24 out of the 32 departments by the countrys main media outlets. Likewise, MOEs political violence reports were essential in providing authorities information for prioritizing prevention and protection mechanisms in election times. Finally, MOE produced an electoral risk map for the 2022 national elections and launched its 2022 electoral observation strategy. As an innovation, this strategy incorporated three differential perspectives with a focus on participation by women, trans persons and people with disabilities.
The MOE has focused its analysis of the political-electoral dynamics in territories especially affected by the conflict, producing reports on the socioeconomic and demographic factors that affect democracy in: a) in 2017 the Transitional local Zones of Normalization where FARC excombatants started the reincorporation process (ZVTNs is its acronym in Spanish); b) the territories with the Development Programs with a Territorial Approach (PDETs is its acronym in Spanish); and c) the Special Transitory Circumscriptions of Peace in 2021.
In 2021 the Constitutional Court allowed elections for Special Transitory Peace Voting Districts (CITREP is its Spanish acronym) in the National Congress election, which includes representation of victims of conflict from the16 most affected regions that were established in the 2016 Peace Agreement. MOE provided technical support to the National Registration Office for the regulation of these Districts and presented two special reports about the challenges for electoral participation in those regions and recommendations to the National Electoral Council (CNE is the acronym in Spanish). In addition to the reports, an important outcome was the adoption by the CNE of these recommendation through resolution 10592.
The MOE also developed the observatory of Women, power and politics. They uses the gender perspective in a cross-cutting way in its investigations, data analysis, public policy proposals, and media and academic incidence activities. In 2019, this group analyzed the obstacles that women face to obtain parity and occupy publicly elected positions. The group also conducted a workshop to train reporters on how to do electoral media coverage with a gender perspective. During 2020 and 2021, the MOE contributed to significant progress for the political participation of women and trans people, supporting both the electoral reform that stablished gender parity in the lists of candidates and the adoption of the Protocol to promote the right to vote of trans people in equal conditions and free of discrimination together with LGBTIQ organizations Fundación GAAT and Caribe Afirmativo. In addition, the MOE produced the protocol to prevent gender-based violence in Colombian political participation and a guide with recommendations to address and prevent this type of violence. these recommendations were both adopted by the CNE through formal resolutions. The Embassy welcomed MOEs efforts to strengthen its work on gender equality and inclusion of LGBTI people.
2. Corruption, politics, and democracy
During the electoral processes, the MOE monitored the campaign financing and published reports widely publicized in the media. In addition. MOE investigated 253 candidates government plans, focusing on six specific variables that should be included in their plans per National Planning Department guidelines: prognosis, ideological platform, shared development vision, flagship strategies or programs, financing options and inclusion of women and LGBTI population. MOE concluded that 32.8% of the analyzed categories received the lowest compliance measurement (not met). In 2021 MOE published two reports on public procurement containing recommendations on how to improve access to information and transparency that were presented to national authorities.
3. Political influence society-state
In 2018 and 2019 The MOE carried out a strict follow-up to the process of political reforms, including reform to the Electoral Code. Within the framework of the Interest Group for Political Reform (GIREPO), different proposals were assessed, and recommendations made to the Congress. In 2021 the MOE presented the document political and electoral proposal of reforms-2022-2026. This document describes the legal framework of current electoral institutions as well as recommendations for reforms that increases transparency and effectiveness in the electoral process, based on the 15 years of MOEs experience in electoral observation. In addition, the MOE participated in three public hearings in the Constitutional Court about a proposed reform to the electoral code and the monitoring of the Law to guarantee political opposition.
The Decree No. 2821 of December 2013 includes the MOE as the sole actor of civil society called to participate in all electoral monitoring commissions. The MOE has been present in electoral monitoring commissions throughout the country. In support of the Immediate Reception Unit for Electoral Transparency (URIEL), the MOE assists subcommittees on electoral issues in the Ministry of the Interior. Electoral follow-up commissions are a space that can impact territorial electoral incidents and present alerts and risks to the authorities for coordinated actions to solve them. 123 of these meetings were held at the national level, with one focusing on violence against women in politics.
With Sida resources, MOE designed a strategy to monitor intolerance and fake news in social media. MOEs hashtag #PolíticaSinViolencia (#PoliticsWithoutViolence) generated 40,000 social media interactions. The second most influential organization in this matter only generated 4,600. As regards communication, MOE was very active in the whole activity period. In 2019 the organization worked on its visibility with an output of 215 graphic pieces that have a visual and graphic identity easily recognizable as MOEs. It also increased its Facebook followers by 5,000, to a total of 25,116. There was a 14.4% public engagement with MOEs social media content. MOE currently has over 40,000 Twitter followers, 4,000 more than 2018. MOE tracked over 5,400 news, making emphasis on the coverage provided to female candidates and the gender bias against them in the media. In 2021 with more than 3,600 news items published in the national media (printed and digital press, TV and radio), 355 interviews on the radio and more than 130 quotes in the national media. In addition, the Director participated, with professors, journalists and analysts, in 20 programs on the TV national channel to analyze political and electoral matters.
The Embassy's assessment is that MOE has achieved the intended outputs. The high quality of their analysis and reports, fluent dialogue with national authorities and the communication strategy have contributed to position this organization as a reference for the media and citizens on electoral matters. As expressed by the external evaluators the MOE has had a high impact in strengthening CSOs capacities, government institutions and the media. MOE has demonstrated good capacity to monitor, evaluate and learn. According to the mid-term review, dated May 2019, MOEs actions have contributed to increase civil society's trust in electoral processes and increase the capacities of social and political organizations, universities and citizens in general to conduct observation and follow-up on electoral processes (UM2017/23132-36).
In addition, the Electoral Risk Maps and the denounces have contributed to General Attorneys Office and the Prosecutors General Office, investigations and captures for electoral irregularities.
The Embassy's assessment is that during the last years the MOE was able to adapt to the changes in the sociopolitical context and still deliver high-quality, high-impact results. The MOE and its platform of 418 regional groups (social organizations, women's, youth, religious, academic, Afro-descendant, indigenous, unions, etc.) is an example of social active participation. They have presence in 587 municipalities through 35 regional offices that have nourish their analysis and recommendations towards authorities.
Based on the good results, the Embassy has decided to start a new contribution to MOE for the period January 2022 to December 2025 as a core support program.
